:::{#thm-deriv-const}
#### Constant rule

If $c$ is constant with respect to $x$, then

$$\deriv{x}c = 0$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-deriv-const-factor}
#### Constant multiple rule

If $a$ is constant with respect to $x$
and $y$ is a differentiable function of $x$, then:
$$\deriv{x}ay = a \derivf{y}{x}$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-deriv-polynomial}
#### Power rule

For every real number $q$ and every $x > 0$:

$$\deriv{x}x^q = qx^{q-1}$$

When $q$ is a positive integer,
the same formula holds for every real $x$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-deriv-log}

#### Derivative of natural logarithm

For every $x > 0$:

$$\dlogf{x} = \frac{1}{x} = x^{-1}$$
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-deriv-exp}
#### derivative of exponential

For every real $x$:

$$\dexpf{x} = \expf{x}$$
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-product-rule}
#### Product rule

If $a$ and $b$ are differentiable functions of $x$, then

$$(ab)' = ab' + ba'$$
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-quotient-rule}
#### Quotient rule

If $a$ and $b$ are differentiable functions of $x$
and $b \neq 0$, then

$$(a/b)' = a'/b - (a/b^2)b'$$
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-chain-rule}
#### Chain rule

If $a$ is a differentiable function of $b$,
and $b$ is a differentiable function of $c$,
then $a$ is a differentiable function of $c$, and

$$\ba
\dif{a}{c} &=
\dif{a}{b} \dif{b}{c}
\\
&= \dif{b}{c} \dif{a}{b}
\ea
$$

or in [Lagrange's notation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Notation_for_differentiation#Lagrange's_notation),
if $g$ is differentiable at $x$
and $f$ is differentiable at $g(x)$:

$$(f(g(x)))' = g'(x) f'(g(x))$$
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#cor-deriv-log-chain}

#### Chain rule for logarithms

If $f$ is differentiable at $x$ and $f(x) > 0$, then

$$
\dif{}{x}\logf{f(x)} = \frac{f'(x)}{f(x)}
$$

:::

::: proof
Apply @thm-chain-rule and @thm-deriv-log:

$$
\ba
\dif{}{x}\logf{f(x)}
&= f'(x) \cd \dlogf{f(x)}
&& \text{(chain rule, with } g = f \text{ and outer function } \log \text{)}
\\
&= f'(x) \cd \frac{1}{f(x)}
&& \text{(derivative of } \log \text{, valid because } f(x) > 0 \text{)}
\\
&= \frac{f'(x)}{f(x)}
&& \text{(multiply)}
\ea
$$
:::

### Linear approximation

For a differentiable function $f$ and a small step $\epsilon$,

$$f(w + \epsilon) \approx f(w) + \epsilon\,\dif{}{w}f(w)$$ {#eq-linear-approx}

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-flat-point}
#### Flat point

A derivative of zero marks a **flat point** (also called a *stationary point*).
A point where the derivative is zero or does not exist is a *critical point*.
:::
